title: Live source permission checks
summary: After retrieval, ask the system of record whether this caller may read each candidate right now. It gives the freshest answer, at the price of latency, load and failure handling.
useIf: Rights are per document or rule-based, change quickly and are owned by another system.
avoidIf: Query volume is high and the source cannot take a call per hit, or an index-side filter already meets the revocation target.

explain.md: A live check treats the index ACL as a hint and the **source of truth as the decision**. The usual shape is a pre-filter that returns a short candidate list, then parallel permission calls for only the top hits, with a deadline and a fail-closed rule. Checking every candidate is rarely affordable, and checking only the hits the user will see is usually enough.

explain.title: Pre-filter, then parallel live checks
explain.alt: A query is pre-filtered to a short candidate list. The top hits are checked in parallel at the source with a deadline. Allowed hits are kept, spare candidates refill gaps, and the result goes to the prompt.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  Q[Query] --> F[(Pre-filter top 20)]
  F --> C[Parallel live checks on top hits]
  C --> K[Keep allowed, refill from spares]
  K --> P[Prompt]
  C -. timeout .-> D[Drop hit, fail closed]

explain.title: Latency of the checks
explain.expr: parallel: max(t_i), capped by the deadline. sequential: sum(t_i)

vars.v: latency of the permission call for hit i

explain.example: Ten checks of 80 ms each cost about 80 ms plus tail when run in parallel and 800 ms when run one after another. Always set a per-call and an overall deadline.

explain.md: Three design choices matter. First, **cache decisions** by principal and document with a TTL shorter than the revocation target, because the TTL is part of your SLA. Second, **fail closed**: if a check times out, hide the document. Azure AI Search's native ACL enforcement does this too: when Microsoft Graph is unavailable it returns a 5xx and no partially filtered result [[r12]]. Third, **delegation** is the cousin of this pattern: the Microsoft 365 Copilot Retrieval API preserves permissions without copying data, but limits calls to 200 per user per hour and 25 results [[r26]].

explain.title: Change feeds are not a live check
explain.md: Microsoft Graph driveItem notifications average under one minute but can take up to six hours, and directory subscriptions expire in under 29 days [[r27]]. Do not promise a revocation SLA tighter than the feed you depend on.

whereToUse: Restricted tiers where a revoked grant must stop working in seconds
Sources with deny rules, sharing links or guests that cannot be copied into an index
A second line of defence on the top hits after an index pre-filter
Systems where an internal policy service already answers can-this-user-read-this

use: Revocation targets are seconds to a minute
Rules are richer than allow lists
Few hits per answer need checking
avoid: Sources with strict per-user rate limits and no caching
Failing open to protect availability for restricted data
flips: Revocation relaxes to hours: drop the live check and rely on the pre-filter
The source gives a retrieval API that honours permissions: delegate instead of checking
Query volume grows 10 times: add a short-TTL decision cache and a circuit breaker

pitfalls.symptom: Answers get slower as users cite more documents
pitfalls.fix: Run them in parallel with a per-call and an overall deadline

pitfalls.symptom: A source outage exposes restricted documents
pitfalls.cause: The code fails open on timeout
pitfalls.fix: Fail closed for restricted tiers and alert on timeout rates

pitfalls.symptom: Users are throttled by the source
pitfalls.cause: Every hit triggers a fresh call
pitfalls.fix: Cache decisions for a TTL shorter than the SLA and batch where the API allows

scenarios.title: Tight latency budget, fast source
scenarios.situation: Retrieval has 300 ms in total. The permission API answers in about 100 ms at the median and 150 ms at p95. Answers use up to five documents, and a revoked grant must stop working within seconds.
unknowns: What is the source's rate limit?
What happens when a hit is dropped?
scenarios.question: How do you add the live check?

options.name: Check about 50 candidates one by one
options.why: Fifty serial calls cost seconds and break the budget.
options.tradeoff: Only plausible for batch jobs with no latency target.

options.name: Pre-filter to 20, check the top 5 in parallel with a 120 ms deadline, refill from spares and fail closed on timeout
options.why: Parallel calls cost about one call plus tail and fit the budget.
options.tradeoff: A slow source hides some documents, so track the timeout rate.

options.name: Check only the single top hit
options.tradeoff: The other cited documents are unchecked, so revocation is stale for them.

flips.if: The source p95 rises to 400 ms
flips.then: Delegate or shorten the live set and lean on the pre-filter.
A short-TTL decision cache can replace many calls.

scenarios.takeaway: Check few hits, in parallel, with a deadline.

scenarios.title: Source quota of 200 requests per user per hour
scenarios.situation: The source API allows 200 permission calls per user per hour. Heavy users run 60 queries an hour and each cites eight documents. Restricted content needs revocation within a minute.
constraints: 480 checks per heavy user per hour
unknowns: Do the same documents recur across queries?
scenarios.question: How do you stay under quota?

options.name: Cache decisions per principal and document for 60 seconds, and check only top hits
options.why: Recurring hits reuse a decision, and the TTL fits the one-minute target.
options.tradeoff: Up to a minute of staleness and a cache to scope and test.

options.name: Cache decisions for 24 hours
options.why: A day-old decision defeats a one-minute revocation target.
options.tradeoff: Fine for general content with a daily SLA.

options.name: Use one broad service identity to check on behalf of all users
options.tradeoff: The check then runs under the service's rights unless it asks about the user explicitly, which risks a confused deputy.

flips.then: Batch the top hits in one call.
Drop the cache and check live.

scenarios.takeaway: A cache TTL is part of the revocation SLA.

scenarios.title: The policy service times out
scenarios.situation: An internal policy service times out on about 2% of calls during peak. The assistant serves a restricted tier and a general tier. Product wants high availability.
unknowns: What does a timeout cost the user?
Is the index ACL fresh enough for the general tier?
scenarios.question: What do you do on timeout?

options.name: Fail closed on the restricted tier, tell the user some sources were unavailable, and fall back to the index ACL on the general tier
options.why: It protects restricted data and keeps general answers flowing.

options.name: Fail open for all tiers to protect availability
options.why: An outage then exposes restricted documents.

options.name: Fail closed for all tiers
options.tradeoff: Needless loss of general answers during timeouts.

flips.if: Timeouts exceed a few percent for minutes
flips.then: Open a circuit breaker and serve the restricted tier from cache or decline.

flips.if: The general tier is also sensitive

scenarios.takeaway: Decide fail-open or fail-closed per tier before the outage.

quiz.q: Ten permission checks each take 80 ms and you run them one after another. How many milliseconds do they add?
quiz.explain: Ten times 80 ms is 800 ms. In parallel the cost is about the slowest call plus tail, around 80 ms, which is why checks should run concurrently with a deadline.

quiz.q: You cache permission decisions to protect a rate-limited source. How long may the TTL be?
options: As long as needed to stay under the quota
No longer than the revocation target for that tier
Exactly one hour for every tier
Until the document is next re-indexed
quiz.explain: The TTL adds staleness on top of everything else, so it must stay inside the revocation target of the tier. Quota pressure, a fixed hour and re-index time are not reasons to exceed it.

flashcards.front: What is the usual shape of a live check?
flashcards.back: Pre-filter to a short list, check the top hits at the source in parallel with a deadline, refill from spares, and fail closed on timeout.

flashcards.front: How does Azure AI Search native ACL behave when Graph is down?
flashcards.back: It fails closed: the service returns a 5xx and no partially filtered result.

flashcards.front: Why must a decision cache TTL be shorter than the revocation target?
flashcards.back: A cached allow stays valid until it expires, so the TTL is part of the revocation SLA.
